To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the effect of language instruction on achievement in language is small and fades away quickly, (ii) the effect of (early) instruction on language on achievement in other skills, such as mathematics and reading, is long-lasting, and (iii) the effect of instruction on language on language skills is long-lasting, but only when the instruction is intensive.
(i) effects of language instruction fade away quickly and (ii) early language instruction affects several other skills in the long run.

(1) language instruction has a positive effect on language skills that fades away quickly, (2) language instruction has positive effects on several nonlanguage skills that are long-lasting and (3) the effects of language instruction spill over to other subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how the allocation of instruction time affects multiple skills.
the allocation of instruction time in schools and the effects of that allocation on student skills.
the question of how to allocate instruction time to subjects in the primary school.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
language instruction should not be allocated more instruction time than other subjects.
the optimal distribution of instruction time depends on the skills that need to be acquired and the extent to which skills are related.
the effects of language instruction are long-lasting and that the effects are not limited to language achievement, but that they also spill over to several other skills.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
language instruction has a positive effect on several skills, but the effect is not as large as one would expect based on short-term effects.
language instruction is important in the early years of primary education, but that its effect on language skills diminishes quickly.
the allocation of instruction time to language instruction is a matter of efficiency, not equity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

schools need to be careful when allocating instructional time to subjects, as it is not only the direct effects of instruction on the subject that matter, but also the long-term effects on other subjects.
the effectiveness of instruction time allocation depends not only on how skills further improve, but also on how skills interact with each other.
the allocation of instruction time across subjects is an important determinant of skill acquisition.
